name: Event-Driven Trading
title: Event-Driven Trading
answer: Event-driven trading is the practice of taking positions because a specific, dated event is expected to change a company's value, such as an earnings release, a merger announcement, a regulatory ruling or a lawsuit outcome. In an AI-focused setting the events include model launches, chip export rules, data licensing deals and antitrust actions against large platforms. The horizon is usually days to months, and the edge comes from judging what the market has already priced rather than from a long-term view of the business.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Event-driven trading is the practice of taking positions because a specific, dated event is expected to change a company's value, such as an earnings release, a merger announcement, a regulatory ruling or a lawsuit outcome. In an AI-focused setting the events include model launches, chip export rules, data licensing deals and antitrust actions against large platforms. The horizon is usually days to months, and the edge comes from judging what the market has already priced rather than from a long-term view of the business.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The desk runs on a market data feed, a news and filings feed, and a calendar of scheduled events, all normalised into one timestamped store. Filings arrive through public archives such as SEC EDGAR, while headlines and press releases come from commercial vendors. Execution sits on a broker or order management system, and the research side is typically Python with pandas and a backtesting library, plus a database for point-in-time prices so that a backtest cannot see data that was not yet public.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by defining the event precisely, then measuring how similar events moved comparable names in the past. Analysts build an expected outcome, compare it with the price and options-implied move, and size a position only when the gap is large enough to cover costs. Much of the effort goes into the data pipeline: aligning announcement times to price ticks, handling halts and gaps, and separating the event effect from the market and sector move on the same day. Machine learning is used mainly for classification and for reading text, not for predicting the price directly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Event-driven strategies sit close to material non-public information, so the boundary between public filings, press coverage and a private tip has to be documented and enforced. Firms keep restricted lists, watch lists and personal trading rules, and in the United States the SEC's insider trading framework and Regulation Fair Disclosure shape what can be acted on and when. Records of the source, timestamp and version of every input matter for both audit and backtest integrity, and merger situations add their own disclosure and competition review steps. This page describes practice only and is not legal, financial or investment advice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward faster and more automated event detection, with language models reading filings and transcripts and flagging candidate events for a human to judge. At the same time, crowded trades around well-telegraphed events compress the available edge, which pushes attention toward smaller and less covered situations. Regulation of AI companies keeps generating new event types, from export controls to copyright suits, and desks that can map those events to affected instruments quickly are likely to keep an advantage.
